Snakebite, first aid: move away from the snake and don't try to catch or kill it. Call emergency services now; if you are alone, call right away and follow their instructions. Keep the person still and calm, lying down, on their side if possible, and stop them from moving around at all; carry them on a makeshift stretcher if you can, and get them to medical care without delay, for antivenom: don't wait for symptoms. Take off rings, watches and bracelets, and loosen clothing near the bite, before swelling starts. Cover the bite with a clean, dry dressing. Mark the edge of the swelling on the skin and write down the time. Do NOT use a tourniquet, do NOT cut the wound, and do NOT suck the venom or put chemicals on it. Don't put ice on it or soak it in water. Don't drink alcohol, and don't take aspirin, ibuprofen or naproxen. If you can do it safely from a distance, take a photo of the snake to help identify it. If the person stops responding or stops breathing normally, start CPR.

Sources: WHO, questions and answers on snakebite envenoming (2019); CDC NIOSH, Venomous Snakes at Work; NHS, Snake bites; healthdirect Australia, Snake bites.

In an emergency, call your local emergency number (911 in the US, 112 in Europe).

Remove wet clothing and wrap them in dry blankets, a sleeping bag or towels, with the head covered. Handle them gently. If they're fully awake, give a warm non-alcoholic drink and something sugary like chocolate; give no drinks to someone who isn't fully awake. You can also warm them skin to skin under dry blankets. Don't use a hot bath, hot-water bottle, heat lamp or fire, don't rub their arms, legs, hands or feet, and don't give alcohol. If they stop breathing normally, start CPR and keep warming them. Call emergency services for anyone you think has hypothermia; don't drive them yourself if an ambulance can come.

Head injury: if they might have hurt their neck (a fall from height, a high-speed hit) or aren't responding, don't move them unless they're in danger; support the head so the head, neck and spine stay in a straight line. If they're not responding and not breathing normally, call emergency services and start CPR. If they're not responding but breathing normally, and they're vomiting or their breathing sounds blocked or gurgling, turn them on their side, keeping the head and spine in line. For a bump, hold an ice pack or frozen peas wrapped in a tea towel on it for short periods; never put ice directly on the skin. An adult should stay with them for the first 24 hours. They should rest, avoid alcohol until they feel better, and avoid contact sport for 3 weeks. Get urgent medical advice if they've been sick once, feel dizzy, take blood thinners, or had been drinking; if told to go to hospital, don't drive yourself. Call emergency services if they were knocked out and haven't woken, can't stay awake, have a seizure, vomit more than once, fell more than 1 metre or 5 stairs, were hit at high speed, have problems seeing, hearing, speaking, walking or with balance, new weakness or numbness, clear fluid from the ears or nose, bleeding from the ears, or changed behaviour.
